newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Q'LAND COTTON EYES GLOBAL GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Q'LAND COTTON EYES GLOBAL GROWTH.

text.p: Queensland Cotton Holdings Ltd has its sights firmly set on further international expansion after sewing up its first major foreign acquisition, the US$43 million purchase of U.S.-based Anderson Clayton Corp.
"Our move into the United States is not the end of our plans," Queensland Cotton's chief executive Richard Haire told Reuters in an interview.
Opportunities for possible partnerships and grower marketing deals in South America, parts of Europe and in Africa, were now on the agenda, Haire said.

Completion of the agreed deal to purchase Anderson Clayton, part of the Swiss-based Volkart Group, is expected on August 30 and will transform Queensland Cotton into the world's biggest ginning company.
Haire said he was very optimistic about cotton marketing and distribution prospects in the United States.
The first year of the new acquisition would be involved in bedding down operations - "the real priority is to reorganise both groups," Haire said.

There were promising prospects the enlarged group would be able to eventually market about one-third of the 750,000 bales to be ginned in the United States, producing an extra A$2.5 million in annual earnings, he said.
Haire said he was confident cost savings and efficiency gains could be achieved in Anderson Clayton's operations in California and Arizona.

Although the two groups ginned about the same output of cotton, the U.S. company's earnings of A$1.9 million for 1996/97 were less than Queensland's Cotton's $13.3 million net profit for the year ended February 28, 1997.
Haire said the outlook for the United States cotton crop this year was very good but it was still early days for the Australian crop prospects.
There was the El Nino effect to consider "and we'll need a bit of rain," he said.

Queensland Cotton earlier told shareholders at the annual meeting that although planting in Australia would not occur until at least October this year, good water supplies, strong prices and favourable conditions generally pointed to a cotton crop for 1997/98 of near three million 500-lb bales.
Industry group, Cotton Australia, has estimated Australia would process a record 2.7 million bales of cotton in 1996/97, equivalent to 612,000 tonnes of cotton.
